meta.title: Compensation
meta.summary: Salary and withholding, the new deductions for tips and overtime, employees versus contractors, stock options, restricted stock and the Section 83(b) election, and accountable plans.

videos.title: Salary, bonuses and withholding
videos.take: Employers deduct reasonable pay; employees are taxed when paid, with tax withheld under the W-4

scenes.say: Compensation is a two-sided deal: the employee is taxed, and the employer deducts. Start with plain salary and bonuses.

scenes.heading: Two sides of a paycheck
scenes.say: The employee includes wages in income when received and pays their half of FICA. The employer deducts the wages, as long as they're reasonable, and pays and deducts its matching half of FICA.

sub: An accrual employer can deduct a bonus
this year if paid by March 15
scenes.say: Timing can differ. An accrual-method employer can deduct a year-end bonus in the year it's accrued if it's paid within two and a half months after year-end, while the cash-method employee isn't taxed until it's paid.

scenes.heading: Form W-4, since 2020
items: Step 2: multiple jobs or a working spouse
Step 4: other income and extra deductions
scenes.say: Withholding is set by Form W-4. Since 2020 it no longer uses allowances. Instead, it asks about multiple jobs, dependents, other income and extra deductions, so withholding comes closer to the actual tax.

sub: On deducting pay to top executives
scenes.say: One limit on the employer side: a public company can't deduct more than a million dollars a year of pay to each of its top executives.

scenes.q: Jake's employer, on the accrual method, declares a $5,000 bonus on December 20, 2026 and pays it February 10, 2027. When does each side report it?
scenes.say: Quick check. Jake's employer, on the accrual method, declares a five thousand dollar bonus on December twentieth and pays it February tenth. When does each side report it? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. The employer deducts it in 2026 under the two-and-a-half-month rule. Jake includes it in 2027, when he's paid.

videos.title: No tax on tips and overtime
videos.take: From 2025 to 2028 workers can deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips and up to $12,500 of overtime premium

scenes.say: The 2025 law promised no tax on tips and overtime. In practice, they're two new deductions, with limits.

Workers in occupations that customarily receive tips can deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips a year from 2025 through 2028. Tips must be voluntary, so automatic service charges don't count. The deduction phases out above $150,000 of modified AGI, or $300,000 joint.

scenes.heading: Jess, a server in Marshall
scenes.say: Jess, twenty-eight, is a server at the restaurant where Sam works. She earns $18,000 of wages and reports $22,000 of tips. After her standard deduction and the tips deduction, her taxable income is only $1,900, and her income tax falls from about $2,620 to $190.

sub: The premium part of FLSA overtime:
scenes.say: The overtime deduction covers only the premium part of overtime required by the Fair Labor Standards Act, the half in time-and-a-half. It's capped at $12,500, or $25,000 on a joint return, with the same phase-out.

scenes.heading: Dan: $30 an hour, 300 overtime hours
scenes.say: Dan, a technician at a Marshall plant, earns thirty dollars an hour and works three hundred overtime hours at forty-five. Only the fifteen-dollar premium counts: $4,500 is deductible.

scenes.q: Which is still taxed under these deductions?
opts: Social Security and Medicare tax on tips
Income tax on the overtime premium
scenes.say: Quick check. Which is still taxed? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Both deductions cut income tax only. Tips and overtime are still wages for Social Security and Medicare.

videos.title: Employee or independent contractor?
videos.take: Control decides worker status, which decides who pays payroll taxes and who withholds

scenes.say: When Nora hires help, is the worker her employee or an independent contractor? The answer decides who pays payroll taxes.

scenes.heading: The IRS looks at control
items: Behavioral: who controls how the work is done
Financial: who supplies tools, bears profit or loss
scenes.say: The IRS looks at control. Behavioral control: does the business direct how the work is done? Financial control: who provides equipment and bears the risk of loss? And the relationship: are there benefits, and is it ongoing?

scenes.heading: The consequences
scenes.say: An employee splits FICA with the employer, and the employer withholds income tax and files a W-2. A contractor pays all of their self-employment tax and makes estimated payments. From 2026, a business must file a 1099-NEC for a contractor paid $2,000 or more, up from $600.
Calling an employee a contractor to save payroll tax is risky. The business can owe the back taxes it should have withheld and paid, plus penalties and interest.

scenes.heading: Nora's two helpers
rows: Own gear and methods, many clients
scenes.say: Nora's second shooter brings her own cameras, works for other photographers and decides how to shoot: a contractor. Her studio assistant works set hours on tasks Nora assigns: an employee.

scenes.q: Nora pays a freelance editor $1,500 in 2026. Must she file a 1099-NEC?
scenes.say: Quick check. Nora pays a freelance editor fifteen hundred dollars in 2026. Must she file a ten ninety-nine N E C? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. From 2026 the threshold is $2,000. The editor must still report the income.

videos.title: Stock options
videos.take: Nonqualified options create ordinary income at exercise; ISOs can turn the whole gain into long-term capital gain

scenes.say: Stock options let employees buy company shares at a fixed price. How they're taxed depends on the type.

When you exercise an option, the bargain element is the share's value minus the price you pay. Kari, Erik's wife, holds options on a thousand shares at twenty dollars, and exercises when the shares are worth fifty: a $30,000 bargain element.

scenes.heading: Nonqualified vs incentive options
scenes.say: With nonqualified options, Kari has $30,000 of ordinary income at exercise, subject to payroll tax, and her employer deducts the same amount. Selling later at seventy gives a $20,000 capital gain. With incentive stock options, there's no regular tax at exercise, and the whole $50,000 is capital gain on sale. But the employer gets no deduction.

scenes.heading: ISO holding periods
items: Otherwise: a disqualifying disposition, taxed like an NQO
scenes.say: To get ISO treatment, Kari must hold the shares two years from the grant and one year from exercise. Selling sooner is a disqualifying disposition, taxed like a nonqualified option.
One catch: the ISO bargain element counts for the alternative minimum tax in the year of exercise, which can bring a surprise AMT bill.

scenes.q: Kari exercises NQOs: 500 shares, exercise price $10, value $25. Income at exercise?
scenes.say: Quick check. Kari exercises nonqualified options on five hundred shares, at ten dollars, when they're worth twenty-five. What income does she have? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. The bargain element is fifteen dollars times five hundred: $7,500 of ordinary income.

videos.title: Restricted stock and the 83(b) election
videos.take: Restricted stock is taxed at vesting unless the employee makes an 83(b) election to be taxed at grant

scenes.say: Restricted stock is real shares, but you lose them if you leave before they vest. When are they taxed? Usually at vesting, unless you choose otherwise.
Under Section 83, restricted stock is taxed as ordinary income when it vests, at its value on that date. The employer deducts the same amount.

scenes.heading: Kari: 1,000 shares, $10 at grant, $40 at vesting
scenes.say: Kari is granted a thousand restricted shares worth ten dollars, vesting in three years, when they're worth forty. Without an election, she has $40,000 of ordinary income at vesting. With an eighty-three B election within thirty days of the grant, she has only $10,000 of ordinary income now, and all later growth is capital gain.

sub: File within 30 days of the grant
scenes.say: The election must be filed within thirty days of the grant. Miss it, and it's gone.

scenes.big: Forfeit, and the tax is lost
scenes.say: The risk: if Kari leaves before the shares vest and forfeits them, she gets no deduction for the $10,000 she already paid tax on. The election is a bet that the shares will rise and that she'll stay.

scenes.q: When is an 83(b) election most attractive?
opts: Value at grant is low and growth is expected
The employee plans to leave soon
scenes.say: Quick check. When is an eighty-three B election most attractive? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. A low value at grant means little tax now, and expected growth becomes capital gain.

videos.title: Employee expenses and accountable plans
videos.take: Unreimbursed employee expenses aren't deductible, so reimbursement through an accountable plan is the tax-efficient route

scenes.say: Jake pays for a conference out of his own pocket. Can he deduct it? Not anymore. Here's why reimbursement matters.

Unreimbursed employee business expenses used to be a miscellaneous itemized deduction. The 2017 law suspended it, and the 2025 law made that permanent. Employees generally can't deduct work costs they pay themselves.

scenes.heading: An accountable plan requires
scenes.say: The answer is an accountable plan. If the expense has a business connection, the employee substantiates it promptly, and any excess advance is returned, reimbursements are tax-free to the employee and deductible by the employer.

scenes.heading: Jake's $2,000 conference
scenes.say: If Jake's employer reimburses his $2,000 conference under an accountable plan, it's tax-free to him. If it pays a flat allowance with no receipts, that's wages. If Jake pays and isn't reimbursed, he gets no deduction at all.
So an employee with regular work costs is better off with an accountable reimbursement than an equal raise. The raise is taxed; the reimbursement isn't.

scenes.q: Jake buys $300 of work boots required by his job and isn't reimbursed. What can he deduct?
scenes.say: Quick check. Jake buys three hundred dollars of work boots his job requires, and isn't reimbursed. What can he deduct? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, nothing. Unreimbursed employee expenses aren't deductible.

warmup: Would you rather have a $5,000 raise or $5,000 of employer-paid health insurance? A $5,000 bonus or $5,000 of company shares?
Draw out tax-free fringes (L5), the new tips/overtime deductions for some workers, and the timing and risk of equity pay (12.4, 12.5).
acts: A cash-method employee earns a $10,000 bonus declared December 15, 2026 and paid January 5, 2027 by an accrual-method employer. A second employer pays a bonus on April 1, 2027. Timing?
First: employer deducts 2026 (within 2½ months), employee includes 2027. Second: paid after March 15, so the employer deducts in 2027.
A bartender with $70,000 MAGI, single, has $30,000 of tips. Tips deduction?
A single worker with MAGI of $170,000 has $10,000 of qualified overtime premium. Deduction?
Nora's assistant: Nora sets hours, provides equipment, trains her, pays hourly. Status and consequences?
Employee: Nora withholds, pays 7.65% FICA, FUTA and Minnesota unemployment, files W-2.
Kari's ISOs: 1,000 shares at $20, exercised at $50, sold 6 months later at $60. Tax result?
Disqualifying disposition: $30,000 ordinary income (bargain element), $10,000 short-term capital gain. Employer deducts $30,000.
A startup grants an engineer 50,000 shares worth $0.10 each, vesting in 4 years. Should she file an 83(b)?
Probably: $5,000 of income now vs potentially large ordinary income at vesting; risk of forfeiture is small in dollars.
case: Sam Ortiz, 20, works at a Marshall restaurant: $3,000 of wages and $6,000 of tips in 2026. The restaurant adds an automatic 18% service charge to parties of eight or more, and Sam received $800 of that. He also photographs events for Nora, who paid him $2,500 and treats him as a contractor, though she sets his schedule and provides the cameras. Maria claims Sam as a dependent.
Which of Sam's receipts are qualified tips?
Is Sam Nora's employee or a contractor? What changes if he is an employee?
Compute Sam's standard deduction and taxable income, before and after the tips deduction.

Qualified tips: $6,000 voluntary tips; the $800 service charge is wages, not tips. With Nora setting hours and providing cameras, Sam looks like an employee; Nora would withhold, pay FICA and issue a W-2 (as a contractor he'd owe SE tax on $2,500 and get a 1099-NEC since it's over $2,000). Standard deduction: earned income 12,300 + 450 = 12,750. Taxable before tips: 12,300 − 12,750 = 0. Tips deduction adds nothing: he already owes no income tax, but still owes FICA. Forms: W-2 from the restaurant (and from Nora if an employee).
exam: Compare the tax treatment of nonqualified stock options and incentive stock options for the employee and employer at grant, exercise and sale.

Grant: nothing for either. Exercise: NQO bargain element is ordinary income (FICA), employer deducts; ISO no regular tax (AMT adjustment), no employer deduction. Sale: NQO gain over FMV at exercise is capital; ISO whole gain is LTCG if held 2 years from grant and 1 from exercise, otherwise disqualifying disposition.
Explain the qualified tips and qualified overtime deductions, including limits, and state what they do not change.

2025–2028; tips: voluntary tips in customarily tipped occupations, up to $25,000; overtime: premium portion of FLSA overtime, up to $12,500 ($25,000 joint); phase-out $100 per $1,000 over $150,000 MAGI ($300,000 joint); SSN required; available to non-itemizers. No effect on FICA.
outcomes: Explain the timing of wages and bonuses for both parties
Apply the tips and overtime deductions
Classify workers as employees or contractors
Decide when an 83(b) election makes sense
Use accountable plans for employee expenses
take: Wages: employee taxed when paid; employer deducts reasonable pay
Tips up to $25,000 and overtime premium up to $12,500, through 2028
Control decides employee or contractor; 1099-NEC at $2,000 from 2026
NQO: ordinary at exercise; ISO: capital gain if held
83(b): pay tax at grant, convert growth to capital gain
Employees can't deduct work costs: reimburse through an accountable plan

ex.q: An accrual-method employer declares a bonus on December 28, 2026 and pays it on April 2, 2027. When does it deduct the bonus?
ex.why: Payment after March 15 misses the 2½-month window, so the deduction waits until 2027.

ex.q: A single server has $30,000 of qualified tips and MAGI of $160,000. What is the tips deduction?
A worker paid $24 an hour works 200 FLSA overtime hours at $36. What is the qualified overtime deduction?

items: Worker can make or lose money
ex.why: Control over the work, finances and relationship decide status.

ex.q: NQOs: 2,000 shares, exercise price $15, value at exercise $40. Ordinary income at exercise?
ISOs are exercised in March 2026 (granted 2023) and the shares are sold in December 2026 at a gain. What is the result?
opts: Disqualifying disposition: bargain element is ordinary income
ex.why: The shares weren't held one year from exercise.

ex.q: Restricted shares worth $5,000 at grant and $45,000 at vesting. With an 83(b) election, how much ordinary income is there in total?
ex.why: With the election, only the value at grant is ordinary income; growth is capital gain on sale.

ex.q: An employer pays employees a flat $200 a month 'car allowance' with no mileage records. How is it treated?
ex.why: Without substantiation it's a nonaccountable plan, so the allowance is wages.
